Those readings are somewhat higher than our target, but based on what you’ve described, this does not sound like an emergency right now. Very high blood pressure emergencies usually involve much more severe symptoms such as chest pain, trouble breathing, severe sudden headache, confusion, or difficulty speaking. For now, I’d like you to check your blood pressure at home if possible (or at the pharmacy) twice a day for the next 5–7 days, once in the morning and once in the evening, sitting and resting for 5 minutes before you take it. Please write down the numbers and send them to me in a follow-up message.

Continue taking your lisinopril as prescribed. Also, watch your salt intake, limit alcohol, and try to get some regular light exercise like walking if you can.

Once I see the home readings, we can decide if we need to adjust your medication or schedule an earlier appointment.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

You have not done anything “wrong”; sometimes diabetes changes over time and what worked before is no longer enough. I’d like us to review your current eating plan, activity, and medications in more detail and talk about options such as adjusting your metformin dose, considering an additional medication, and looking at meal timing.

This type of change usually does not require an urgent switch to insulin, but in some cases we do add insulin or another medicine if sugars remain high despite other steps. Please schedule an appointment (in person or video) in the next 2–4 weeks so we can go over your glucose readings, diet, and medications and make a plan together.

In the meantime, continue your current medications as prescribed and keep up with your evening walks; if you are checking blood sugars at home, bring or send a log of the readings with dates and times.

John

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi John,

Thanks for reaching out and for describing what has been going on with your sleep in detail.

It’s not uncommon in the first few weeks of starting sertraline to notice some temporary side effects such as feeling more on edge or having changes in sleep. These usually improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts, but I understand that the combination of trouble falling asleep, early awakenings, and feeling exhausted is very frustrating.

For now, I don’t want you to stop the sertraline on your own, since you are still early in the course, but I do think we should adjust the plan. One option is to move your sertraline dose to the morning if you are currently taking it later in the day, as this sometimes helps with sleep. I also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule (waking and going to bed at the same times each day), avoiding screens and work emails for at least an hour before bedtime, and limiting caffeine after noon if possible.

If you notice any severe side effects such as thoughts of harming yourself, feeling out of control, or new or worsening agitation you can’t manage, please call our office right away or go to the emergency room.

Please send me an update in about 1–2 weeks letting me know if the sleep is any better with these changes, and we can decide then whether to adjust the dose, switch medications, or consider a short course of a sleep aid.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

Sam

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Sam,

Thank you for your message and for explaining how much your knees have been affecting your work and daily activities.

From what you describe, it sounds like your osteoarthritis pain has progressed and is no longer well controlled with acetaminophen alone. The X-rays from 6 months ago already showed moderate to severe wear-and-tear changes, and it is common for symptoms to gradually worsen over time.

You have not done anything wrong or “waited too long”—these changes tend to build up over years, and our goal now is to find the best combination of treatments to help you function as well as possible.

In addition to acetaminophen, options we can consider include topical anti-inflammatory gel applied to the knees, a supervised physical therapy program to strengthen the muscles around the joint, a knee brace for support, and, if appropriate given your other health conditions, short courses of an oral anti-inflammatory medication. In some cases, steroid injections into the knee can also provide temporary relief.

Knee replacement surgery is usually considered when pain is significantly limiting daily activities and more conservative measures are no longer helping, but it is not the only option and it is not something we would rush into without a full evaluation.

Please schedule an appointment with me in the next 2–4 weeks so we can examine your knees, review your prior imaging, and talk through these options in more detail. In the meantime, continue using acetaminophen as directed (not exceeding the total daily dose we discussed), try to avoid activities that involve prolonged kneeling or squatting, and use ice packs after heavier activity if that provides relief.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

[Patient]: Hi Dr. Rivera,

About two weeks ago I noticed a red, bumpy rash on the inside of my right forearm. At first it just looked a little dry and itchy, but over the last week it’s spread further down toward my wrist and up toward my elbow.

It’s pretty itchy, especially at night, and I’ve caught myself scratching it in my sleep. I tried some over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and switching soaps, but it doesn’t seem to be going away.

I work in a warehouse and sometimes handle boxes that are dusty or have been in storage a long time, so I’m wondering if it could be something I’m coming into contact with. I’m also a bit worried it could be something more serious like shingles or some kind of skin cancer, even though it doesn’t really hurt, just itches.

I’m feeling a little self-conscious because it’s visible when I wear short sleeves, and a coworker asked me today if it was contagious, which freaked me out. Do I need to come in to have it looked at, or is there something stronger I can try at home?

Thanks,
Eric

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Eric,

Thank you for your message and for describing what has been going on with the rash on your arm.

From what you are describing — an itchy, red, bumpy rash on the inner forearm that has been spreading slowly over about two weeks and is more itchy than painful — this sounds more consistent with a form of eczema or contact dermatitis than with shingles or skin cancer. Shingles usually causes clusters of painful blisters in a band on one side of the body, and skin cancers are typically not this itchy and do not appear so suddenly.

The fact that you work around dusty boxes and may be coming into contact with different materials makes a contact reaction possible. In addition to avoiding any obvious new products (such as soaps, lotions, or gloves) that might be irritating the skin, I would suggest using a gentle fragrance-free moisturizer on the area twice daily and continuing a low-strength steroid cream for a short period.

If you have been using 1% hydrocortisone once or twice a day for a full 1–2 weeks without any improvement, or if the rash starts to blister, ooze, become very painful, or you notice spreading to other areas, we should see you in person to examine it and consider a stronger prescription cream or other treatments.

Please also let us know right away if you develop fever, feel generally unwell, or see red streaks going up the arm, as those would be reasons to be seen more urgently.

Otherwise, if the rash is not improving over the next 1–2 weeks despite gentle skin care and avoiding irritants, please schedule an in-person visit so we can take a closer look.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

Over the past week I’ve been getting these spells where my heart suddenly starts pounding out of nowhere. It usually lasts a few minutes and then settles down, but while it’s happening I feel a little lightheaded and almost like I can’t catch my breath.

It’s been happening maybe once a day, sometimes when I’m just sitting and reading, and it’s starting to really scare me. I keep worrying I’m going to have a heart attack or that something was missed on my tests.

Karen

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Karen,

Thank you for your message and for describing these episodes in detail.

From what you’ve shared so far, these brief spells of heart pounding that resolve on their own after a few minutes, with your blood pressure otherwise well controlled and a normal EKG and labs at your last visit, are less suggestive of an immediate heart attack. However, it is important that we learn more about the pattern to decide what further evaluation is needed.

Amlodipine does not typically cause rapid heart rhythms, but some people can feel more aware of their heartbeat when starting a new blood pressure medication or when they are anxious about their heart. I’d like you to keep a simple log for the next 1–2 weeks: note the time of each episode, what you were doing right before it started, how long it lasts, and whether you have any associated symptoms such as chest pain, pressure, shortness of breath at rest, fainting, or pain going to your jaw or arm.

If at any point you develop severe chest pain or pressure, trouble breathing that does not improve quickly, fainting, or symptoms that feel very different or much more intense than what you’ve described, please call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

Otherwise, please send me the log after 1–2 weeks, and we can decide whether to bring you in sooner for an exam, repeat EKG, or consider a heart monitor to look for an abnormal rhythm. In the meantime, you can continue your amlodipine as prescribed, and it is generally safe to keep up with light to moderate walking as long as you stop and rest if you feel unwell.

Best,
Dr. Rivera
